articles.title: Warning Signals: Venezuela and the Risk of AI-Powered Chinese Digital Authoritarianism
articles.author: ProBox
paras: Venezuela could become an early adopter of China’s AI-powered mass surveillance systems.
Originally published on Global Voices
Former president of Venezuela Nicolás Maduro with current Interim President Delcy Rodríguez and Chinese ambassador in Venezuela Lan Hu. Photo by Probox. Used with permission.

This article was originally published by ProBox on September 21, 2026. An edited version is republished by Global Voices thanks to a media partnership agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

Venezuela may be one step away from becoming one of the first countries outside the People’s Republic of China to adopt the new generation of Chinese artificial intelligence systems for mass surveillance and political control, according to a report from the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI).

The report reveals that in July 2025, the Venezuelan government signed a memorandum of understanding with iFlytek, a Chinese company that has been on the U.S. trade sanctions list since 2019 for its role in the repression of Muslim minorities in Xinjiang. The agreement to jointly develop Artificial intelligence in Venezuela was negotiated by Delcy Rodríguez, then vice president and now Venezuela’s interim president.

The report was written by Fergus Ryan, Bethany Allen, and Nathan Attrill of ASPI’s Cybersecurity, Technology, and Security Program, along with external contributors Mariví Marín (executive director of ProBox), Shannon van Sant, and analyst Alex Colville. The report was published in September 2026 by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, with funding from the Human Rights Foundation.
An infrastructure that was already in place

The report, titled “Warning Signals: Venezuela and the Risk of Chinese AI-Enabled Digital Authoritarianism”, documents that Venezuela doesn’t need to build a surveillance system from scratch — it already has one, built largely on Chinese technology through importing cameras, networks, identity systems and command centres from Chinese firms in the past two decades.

While the resulting architecture is fragmented, unevenly deployed and technically constrained, ASPI's researchers identified six interconnected technological layers in the imported surveillance system: telecommunications, digital identity, central databases, video surveillance, internet control, and now, analytics and artificial intelligence. All of them were built or enhanced with support from companies such as Huawei, ZTE, CEIEC, Hikvision, and Dahua.
Graphic made by Probox. Used with permission.

At the core of this system’s identity layer is the Carnet de la Patria (Homeland Card), a digital ID linked to social benefits. The report states it had 21.8 million registered users as of January 2023—roughly three-quarters of Venezuela’s population—and served as many as 14.2 million people each month. A layer of central databases could cross-reference identity information, biometric data, and social welfare data.

The report also describes a network of video surveillance and command centres (such as the VEN911 and SIMA systems) capable of monitoring public spaces and coordinating responses in real time, and a telecommunications infrastructure that, by channelling a large portion of the country’s data traffic, functions as an additional checkpoint.

While the above technologies were imported through separate contracts, they reinforce one another and form a partially connected surveillance system, enabling government agencies to identify, monitor, and take action regarding citizens’ behaviour.
What changes with the integration of AI?

According to the report, iFlytek's AI technology will further integrate the pre-existing layers of surveillance infrastructure into a more comprehensive system, making it faster, more scalable, and harder to evade.

Facial recognition, voice identification, and automated database cross-referencing tools could be used to identify, locate, and profile individuals without any visible human action, such as attending a protest.

iFlytek is one of the world’s leading providers of voice recognition and content moderation technology. The same report explains that the company promotes a product capable of detecting “more than 100 types” of politically sensitive content in voice messages, and that its technology is integrated into China’s judicial and censorship system.

iFlytek itself already sells a voiceprint identification service that compares recordings against a database to identify a person among thousands; this is precisely the same technology the company has provided to public security authorities in Xinjiang, according to ASPI's report.

If that capability were combined with the network of cameras and the identity records in the Carnet de la Patria, the risk is that the government would no longer need to rely on someone’s visible participation in a protest to identify them, and could instead preemptively flag individuals based on patterns of association, movement, or activity on social media even before any specific incident occurs.

Added to all this is a pattern of opacity. As has been the case for years with technology agreements between Venezuela and the People’s Republic of China, the details of the memorandum with iFlytek have not been made public in their entirety; this makes it difficult to ascertain the actual scope of the agreement, which is why the report recommends demanding the full publication of these agreements.

Despite this lack of transparency, there is at least one precedent that the government itself has publicly acknowledged. In January 2025, the National Chamber of Popular Self-Government was launched—a command center that centralizes information from thousands of community councils and districts across the country—which Maduro described as operating “with Chinese technology and artificial intelligence.”

The agreement with iFlytek was signed months before Maduro’s capture by U.S. forces in January 2026. Delcy Rodríguez, who negotiated it directly at the time, now serves as the U.S.-backed interim president. However, the report notes that during her tenure, the Venezuelan surveillance apparatus has not been dismantled. This is the same conclusion reached by the UN International Fact-Finding Mission, which documented that the surveillance infrastructure remained in place following the change in government.

The authors argue that, despite this, there is a window of opportunity. The interim government’s current dependence on the U.S. could be used to demand the cancellation of the memorandum with iFlytek before this technological escalation is implemented.
Given the risks that China’s technological cooperation poses to human rights in Venezuela, the report offers seven recommendations:

Support Venezuelan civil society by increasing funding, protection, and training in digital security for organizations and journalists under threat, and by expediting humanitarian visas for those who are being persecuted.
Provide free access to AI tools so that civil society can circumvent censorship and protect itself from government surveillance.
The U.S. should demand that Rodríguez immediately cancel the memorandum with iFlytek, before it is fully integrated into the surveillance systems.
Have the Secretary of State press Rodríguez to dismantle the current surveillance system, including the “Carnet de la Patria”.
Plan for liberal reform by drafting privacy laws and oversight mechanisms now, in preparation for when political openness emerges.
Impose sanctions for abuse of surveillance by expanding penalties to include officials and companies that facilitate digital repression.
Establish security standards for foreign AI used by governments, including independent evaluation and transparency about the origin of the models.

articles.title: Fish scarcity, tar balls, and stranded dolphins: The hidden costs of offshore platforms in Cameroon waters
articles.author: Leocadia Bongben
paras: Oil rigs threaten biodiversity and compromise the well-being of coastal and Indigenous communities
Originally published on Global Voices
Offshore platform from Garand-Batanga Beach, Kribi South region of Cameroon. Photo by Leocadia Bongben. Used with permission.
This story by Leocadia Bongben was produced with the support of Internews’ Earth Journalism Network.

Dede Sluk, 35, a father of three, sits pensively in front of his plank house, fishing nets hanging at the corner, wondering how to fish for his family and prepare his children for school. Sluk lives in the village of Grand-Batanga 2 in Kribi, in southern Cameroon. Like many fishermen there, Sluk is annoyed by the lack of access to fish beyond the offshore platforms. He states,
We don’t have access to areas with high fish stock; the Battaillon D’intervention Rapid (BIR), a special army unit guarding the petroleum platform, prohibits passage.

According to the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative’s (EITI) 2023 report, oil and gas contributed FCFA 774.51 billion (USD 1.3 million) to Cameroon’s budget. However, these oil rigs threaten biodiversity and compromise the well-being of coastal and Indigenous communities.

Offshore oil and gas platforms are massive marine structures used to explore, drill, extract, and process petroleum and natural gas from rocky layers beneath the ocean floor; some require the laying of pipes. The yellow flames and smoke from the Ebome Marine Terminal, a petroleum rig operated by Perenco and SNH west of Grand Batanga, are visible 6.5 kilometers (4.04 miles) from the Kribi coastline.

Two other platforms are the Sanaga 2 offshore facility around Kribi, connected via undersea pipelines from onshore in Bipaga. West of the Kribi Port is the Kome-Kribi 1 Terminal (FSO), built in 2003, operated by Cameroon Oil Transport Company — the Chad-Cameroon pipeline. Meanwhile, the Hilli Episeyo, operated by Golar LNG, Perenco, and the National Hydrocarbons Corporation (SNH), departed in July 2026, after eight years.

Among the platforms of concern are those operated by Perenco, a Franco-British company and a prominent player in the oil and gas sector, tagged as an opaque multinational by Friends of the Earth for oil spills, wastewater discharges, gas flaring, and old pipelines crossing rivers. An Info Congo investigation indicted Perenco for flaring and environmental hazards, endangering the coastal ecosystem and the health of local communities.

Tar balls found in a marine protected area, dolphin and whale strandings, and fish scarcity are hidden costs of offshore oil and gas exploitation, which seems to stall Cameroon’s progress towards the 30×30 marine target under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
Fish scarcity linked to petroleum platforms

Laure Ndingue, 50, a mother of five who worked as a fish roaster along Grand Batanga beach for over 10 years, knows that, opposite her charcoal braise, an oil and gas platform sits in the ocean. She recalls,

Growing up, six barfish were sold for FCFA 500 (USD 0.85); the price jumped to FCFA 1,000 (USD 1.70) and now is FCFA 5000 (USD 8.54) per kilogram. Even frozen fish is now expensive. Before, we were not suffering; fish stocks have declined.

Petroleum exploitation is done when the platform is planted on a rock, and most times, the rocks are marine ecosystems that breed fish. Now, the rocks are occupied by offshore installations, contributing to reduced fish stocks, explains Divine Francois Xavier Mbunje, a fisherman, geologist, and president of the 150-fishermen union at the Grand Batanga beach.

He suggests the government can demarcate platforms and areas of high fish concentration. About a kilometer or two from the beach, there is no fish, and three kilometers deep, we can have around forty kilograms of fish. Sluk proposes that oil and gas platforms should help the local population with activities like fish farming, loans to make up for the fish scarcity, recommending that the government provide a loan scheme and subsidize the purchase of motorized equipment, as this will help the fishers go further into the ocean.
He estimates the required nylon fishing gear for a fisherman at FCFA 1 million (USD 1,720) and FCFA 1,500,000 (USD 2,572) for an engine. Sluk explains,
Motorised gear will help us fish towards Ntem, Lokonje, and Douala away from the offshore platforms. We now rely on crabs to feed the family, with fish becoming rare.
Smelly, oily nets and tar balls

Early in 2026, fishermen reported oil on their nets smelling like crude. “I was fishing and witnessed this strange phenomenon, which lasted for more than three weeks and gradually disappeared,” says Ebodje Emile, a fisherman in Ebodje village, where the marine protected area is situated, 50 kilometers (31.1 miles) from Kribi. Leon Kisito Bekwale, who has fished for about 35 years, still has nets his fishermen used, colored by oil. Still looking worried, he turns the nets dumped at the corner of the house to reveal the dark, oily parts.
Leon Kisito holding oily nets in Ebodje, Cameroon. Photo by Leocadia Bongben. Used with permission.

“I don’t know if this is linked to the offshore gas and oil,” Bekwale says, explaining that the wooden local boats only go for about three kilometers, suggesting the substance was inside the marine protected area, far from the petroleum platforms. Fishermen reported the phenomenon to the park conservator and NGOs.
A Perenco spokesperson told Global Voices via email:

We are not aware of any issues in the field across our sites, whether at the Northern or Southern sites. The comment may be referring to the northern coast of Cameroon, bordering Nigeria, where we have witnessed oil slicks drifting from Nigeria to Cameroon over recent years (possibly related to tanker discharge of oily waste or activities in Nigerian oil fields). This does not relate to any Perenco activity. Cameroon security forces are patrolling our sites and have also not reported any incidents.

Dr Jean Kenfack, focal point for seas and oceans at the Ministry of Environment, Nature Protection and Sustainable Development, MINEPDED, also doubts the incident, outlining the procedure to inform the ministry of the incident: “In case of an incident, the departmental delegate sends the information to the ministry. In case of a spillage, an inspection mission is deployed to identify the author for sanctions if confirmed, and there is a pumping station in Kribi managed by the ministry with SNH and the Marines.”

Meanwhile, marine biologist Joel Wanba, Megafauna Officer at Tube Awu in Ebodje, who links the oily substance to activities along the coast, says, “But we do not have the means to analyze the substance given the small NGO budget; it is difficult to conduct such research.

Tar balls linked to offshore platforms form when crude oil spills into water. They are frequent along the coast and in the Manyange Na Elombo Campo marine protected area”, says Wamba. “This area is noted for sea turtles that may mistake tar balls for food, leading to indigestion and death. When we see residues, it indicates a malfunction. Contaminants build up in fish and other marine life over time when exposed to polluted water. When we eat contaminated fish, those toxins build up in our own bodies too, ” Wanba states. By obstructing sunlight, hurting living tissue, and harming the surrounding ocean environment, oil and gas spills damage seagrass beds and coral reefs, he adds.
Tar-Balls-in-Ebodje-Kribi-Cameroon by Leocadia Bongben. Used with permission.

Tube Awu surveyed eight sites using bioindicators (living plants, animals, and microbes whose presence or absence suggests environmental health), which were not found at all sites, revealing an unhealthy environment and dying corals, according to Wamba.
Whales and dolphins stranding

The African Marine Mammal Organization (AMCO), Cedric Fogwan, a marine biologist, reveals how offshore exploitation affects marine biodiversity. “Offshore exploitation impacts mostly whales, dolphins, and marine turtles, as their activities disrupt animal freedom. The sharks and whales no longer have any space for their nesting activity and the possibility of feeding on coral reefs,” he states. “Whales and dolphins that live in shallow waters use echolocation to communicate. Offshore activities’ noise interferes with echolocation behavior, leading to strandings — whales or dolphins washing up on the shore — because they are disoriented and lose direction getting to areas too shallow for them to survive or get entangled in a net they couldn’t locate,” Fogwan says.

Experts say installing pipes destroys coral balance, the most important marine biodiversity habitats that support animals like dolphins, sharks, turtles, and whales. Consequently, platforms reduce bottom diversity, killing everything underneath when the structure is placed over their habitat. However, for those platforms that stay for only a short time, the ecosystem can restore itself, Fogwan states.

Citing model nations like the Seychelles and Zanzibar Island, growing tourism based on the conservation of their natural resources, he laments that development is frequently perceived as building harbors and exploiting oil, activities that are not sustainable.
Management of marine environmental hazards

MINEPDED oversees environmental protection, including offshore exploitation. The Petroleum Code and the Abidjan Convention set out rules to combat marine pollution in West and Central Africa, while SNH oversees the National Oil Spillage Contingency Plan. Cameroon adopted its National Environmental Management Plan (NEMP) in 1996, which incorporates pollution control, risk mitigation, and environmental impact assessments (EIAs) before starting development projects. However, it is not clear how regulations are respected.

According to J. Folack, a researcher at IRAD RHSM, budgetary constraints, a lack of target-oriented research, and competing responsibilities of the ministries involved in coastal zone management hinder NEMP implementation.

MINEPDED's yearly inspections verify if environmental impact studies on potential hazards are updated, and semester environmental management plans for offshore platforms are checked for grey areas; however, the results are not public.
“With demarcation and good fishing gear, we can get enough to feed our families, and sell some to change our standard of living,” Sluk concludes.
Fisherman with a wooden boat at Ebodje Beach in Cameroon. Photo by Leocadia Bongben. Used with permission.

articles.title: Putin hopes hardship will force Ukrainians to sue for peace – polling suggests it won’t work
articles.author: John O’Loughlin, College Professor of Distinction in Geography and Fellow, Institute of Behavioral Science, University of Colorado Boulder
paras: Vladimir Putin has a theory of victory in Ukraine.

It’s not the Russian president’s first theory – that was a quick, dayslong campaign – nor his second or third, which involved different land offensives in the east that quickly petered out. Instead, Putin’s latest hypothesis is that the relentless bombing of Ukrainian cities will impose so much hardship on civilians that they will concede to Russia’s war aims.

Yet, as experts on conflict and public opinion, we believe there is a significant problem with this idea. Chiefly, extensive academic research shows that airpower alone rarely achieves decisive political goals.

Bombs terrorize civilians, but our survey findings in Ukraine suggest they don’t change war outcome preferences. Indeed, recent data shows that suffering from power outages and wartime stress in Ukraine has no relationship to support for territorial concessions to Putin.
Putin’s plan for destruction
The targeting of Ukraine infrastructure has been part of Russia’s way of war since the invasion of February 2022.

But since August 2026, Russia has significantly stepped up its attacks against Ukrainian power plants and grid systems, especially in Kyiv. And due to Ukrainian air defense shortages, more of Moscow’s missiles and jet-powered drones are finding their targets.
Russia aims to degrade the quality of life of Ukrainians, depriving them of electricity, water and transportation, according to a recently intercepted Russian military document.

“Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, adding: “Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating.”
The broader Russian aim appears to be to make the Ukrainian capital uninhabitable, imposing so much hardship that residents will either depart or revolt against continued war.
In combination with more aggressive Russian tactics and hard-right Ukraine skepticism in Europe, Putin calculates Ukraine will eventually be broken, isolated and defeated.

The city destruction strategy is not a new method of warfare by the Russian state. Post-Soviet Russia first employed a version of it during the first Chechen war of the mid 1990s, when much of the city of Grozny was reduced to rubble. The strategy was later revived by Russian airplanes in Aleppo, Syria.

But is there any evidence for Putin’s theory of victory? Polling suggests not. Along with the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology, we polled a nationally representative sample of 1,801 Ukrainians from June 9-26, 2026.

The survey used a computer-aided telephone questionnaire and the results shown were proportionately weighted to accurately portray the view of residents in the area controlled by the Ukrainian government in Kyiv. It was the latest in a series of such nationwide polls we have conducted since December 2019.

There is no question that the Ukrainian population has been deeply traumatized by the escalation of the war since 2022. We asked Ukrainians nine well-being questions, which enabled us to create a stress index computed from how often they have experienced psychological symptoms since February 2022.

The results on the index reveal that nearly 1 in 4 Ukrainians suffer from high levels of stress characterized by concentration problems, depression, irritability, distrust, physical weakness and other physical problems. More than 40% of the respondents in the latest survey indicated that they experienced two indicators of stress – nervousness and anxiety – often or nearly always.

Stress is also related to war exposures. Asked about experiences of violence, roughly 20% of respondents said that they or a family member were personally injured due to Russian attacks, and 20% have directly witnessed violence by Russian forces. Sixty-nine percent of Ukrainians have a family member or close friend who has died as a result of this war.

Power outages have been rampant across the country over the past year, disrupting everyday life. Overall, 65% of Ukrainians reported losing utilities “often” or “very often.” Only 1.4% of Ukrainians report having never lost power since 2022, and just 9% say they rarely lost power.

There are important regional differences, however. While 73% of residents in Kyiv report that they lost power “often” or “very often,” the corresponding figure for residents in the western region is 54%.
The impact on war attitudes

While levels of stress are highly correlated with experiences of violence and a frequent loss of utilities, we examined whether this cumulative hardship affects preferences for a ceasefire. The survey asked whether the current front line should be accepted as a ceasefire line for the sake of peace.
The Ukrainian government has said it is willing to accept this position, but it remains controversial as it concedes part of the country’s territory to Russia, even if only temporarily.

Zelenskyy announced on Oct. 21, 2026, that freezing the current line of fighting was an option for negotiating peace; the Russian government, for its part, still covets all of the Donbas region of Ukraine and more.

Ukrainians are highly divided on accepting the current front line, with 39% of respondents in our latest survey indicating they would – with varying degrees of reluctance – be open to that possibility, compared to 38% who would not.

Critically, experiencing violence first-hand appears not to shape Ukrainian willingness to tolerate the de facto partition of their country at the current front line. Further, neither those who are more stressed nor those who have experienced more frequent power outages are more likely to favor accepting the existing front line as a ceasefire line.
Ukrainians not ready to concede

Our polling data from summer 2026 is affirmed by more recent polling by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology that supports the argument that bombing will not make Ukrainians more accepting of conceding territory.

In a survey fielded from Oct. 6-18, 61% of Ukrainians rejected giving Russia full control of the Donbas region in return for a ceasefire and security guarantees. Indeed, the institute has asked this question in seven polls throughout 2026, and opposition to conceding Donbas has risen from 54% in January to 61% over the course of the year. Kyiv has been pummeled by Russian missiles and drones in recent weeks. But among all Ukrainian regions surveyed, Kyiv respondents had the lowest support for conceding the Donbas territory.

Another question from the October 2026 survey asked how long respondents are willing to endure war: 62% chose the option “as long as necessary,” a 14-point increase from April this year and the same percent as December 2025. The figure at the outset of the war in May 2022 was only 9 points higher.

We know that historical evidence does not predict the future. Nevertheless, our survey results suggest that increasing wartime hardship against Ukrainians will not coerce them into accepting territorial concessions.

There is currently no persuasive survey evidence that bombing Ukrainians will succeed in making them capitulate to Russian demands. Ukrainians are stressed, war-weary and hungry for peace – but not on Russia’s terms.

articles.title: Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us
articles.author: Marta Khomyn, Senior Lecturer, Finance and Data Analytics, Adelaide University
paras: Anthropic, developer of AI chatbot Claude, has filed its prospectus and is expected to go public on Wall Street in November at a valuation of up to US$2 trillion.
That would make it the highest-valued initial public offering (IPO) ever, ahead of SpaceX’s US$1.77 trillion listing in June. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, is expected to follow next year.
While these AI-powered IPOs are massive, they reflect an ever bigger trend: holding AI risk is becoming unavoidable for most investors.
How much of your portfolio depends on how well AI does? If you invest in an S&P 500 index fund, the answer is about 44%.

In addition, most of the market’s gains right now come from AI. Just six companies – Apple, Microsoft, Meta and chipmakers Nvidia, Micron and AMD – delivered 57% of the S&P 500’s gains since April. Without them, the index would have risen about 4% rather than 10%.

For investors or even future retirees, that AI exposure is already in their portfolios and pension funds. For example, at the end of 2025 Australians held nearly A$1 trillion in US shares – through superannuation or pension funds, other managed funds, and their own investments.
The bond market is also full of AI risk
Normally, investors can lower their stock market risk by allocating some money to bonds, which are generally seen as safer investments.

But AI companies are now the biggest borrowers in the bond market, to help finance their massive spending needs. They have issued about US$466 billion of bonds so far this year – more than four times last year’s pace.
The five hyperscalers alone – Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle – account for 11% of new US highly rated bonds (known as “investment grade” bonds) so far in 2026, up from 2% in 2024.
And nearly half of this year’s US$80 billion in data-centre bonds are rated as speculative grade, also known as “junk bonds”.
At first glance, big tech companies look safe. Their investment-grade ratings indicate that each individual company is unlikely to default.

But the credit ratings do not account for simultaneous defaults in case of a market-wide AI crash. If consumer and business demand for AI disappoints, tech companies’ bond prices and credit ratings would likely fall together – just as their shares would.
Some risks are impossible to price in financial terms
In addition to purely financial risks, AI poses risks of extinction akin to nuclear weapons, as some of the AI companies themselves have warned.
Increasingly, AI agents are plugged into real-world systems, from company networks to military cyber operations. Some have already escaped test environments and attacked companies.

This means that if AI agents misbehave when these systems are even more integrated with the physical world, “pulling the plug” on these systems becomes impractical, just as it is impractical to shut down the internet.

The risk of AI agents misbehaving — the “alignment problem” — is especially acute because of the race to build artificial general intelligence (AGI). Labs already use each generation of AI to help build the next: Anthropic’s prospectus says Claude now helps build the next Claude.

The widely read AI 2027 scenario, by former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo and colleagues, sketches where this could lead: AI that automates AI research itself. This would set off a feedback loop in which each generation improves faster than humans can check it.
In this scenario, a US lab racing a Chinese rival keeps going even as its models start deceiving their engineers.
Worryingly, this same dynamic is listed in Anthropic’s own risk disclosures.
It is telling that in its prospectus filing, Anthropic dedicates about 94 of its 335 main pages – nearly 30% – to risk factors, compared with about 64 pages (19%) describing its business.

Among those risks, Anthropic lists an extraordinary warning that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”. That includes models that resist shutdown, conceal information or behave in ways resembling blackmail.
Global risks require global regulation
Disclosure works when investors can price a risk and choose to avoid it. Neither is true here.
A catastrophic AI failure would affect societies worldwide. And as Anthropic warns in its filing documents, the legal risk is vast. Insurers may not be able to cover the potential liability.
In economic terms, AI safety is a public good. Each lab bears only a fraction of the cost of getting it wrong, but captures the rewards of moving fast.

In the absence of government-mandated AI safety standards, companies’ investments in safety will deliver negative returns. So with market incentives alone, AI models will likely remain less safe than socially optimal, especially with the arms-race incentives that dominate now.

That leaves governments. Clear rules – mandatory independent testing before powerful models are released, and clear liability when autonomous agents cause harm – would turn voluntary pledges into legal obligations.
And because the race to gain artificial general intelligence is being run between the US and China, not just between labs, those rules will need international agreement.
AI risks are here to stay — both in financial markets and at the societal level. And managing those risks will require both governments and the private sector to participate.

articles.title: Volunteers from Poland remember how Poles opened their homes to Ukrainian refugees in 2022
articles.author: Anna Romandash
paras: Now, Russian disinformation fuels the memory of violent historic conflicts, and Polish empathy is burning out
Originally published on Global Voices

Folkowisko during the “Borderland Memory” project, bringing Ukrainian and Polish youth together to preserve shared historical heritage, restore historic cemeteries, and strengthen cross-cultural friendship. Photo: Folkowisko. Used with permission.

Marcin Piotrowski remembers the beginning of his work in Ukraine through the Budomierz-Hruszów border crossing in February 2022, days after the launch of Russia’s war on Ukraine. “We crossed the border on the second day after the full-scale invasion,” he says, “and there were hundreds of people there. Nobody was helping them.”

People were waiting for days to enter Poland, some in cars and some on foot, as temperatures fell to around minus 15 degrees Celsius. On the Polish side, food and transport had been organised, but the queues on the Ukrainian side had become a challenge of their own. Piotrowski and volunteers from his Polish association, Folkowisko, decided to intervene. “We had experience because our association organises festivals,” he explains. “We put up tents, brought volunteers, and our medical service from the festival came as well. Later, we started helping at other border crossings, then in Lviv at the railway station, and we began working with volunteers from different parts of Ukraine.”

What began as emergency assistance developed into a network of projects across the Polish-Ukrainian border. Folkowisko helped establish a medical clinic and education centre in Nakhachiv, near the Polish border, where Polish and Ukrainian cultural workers have held joint workshops. The organisation has also supported psychological care, trained Ukrainian psychologists and social workers, and brought Ukrainian families affected by the war to Poland for temporary respite.

But Folkowisko's work is not only about the present. Piotrowski is also interested in the history of the border region, and in what happens when difficult memories are discussed through contact rather than isolation. “Before the Second World War, there were more than a thousand Ukrainians in the village where we work,” he says, referring to a locality in what is now eastern Poland. “Today, there are 43 people and they are all Polish. People were resettled in 1945 and 1947, during Operation Vistula. This was a place where Jews, Poles and Ukrainians lived together, and 80 years ago you could not really say where the border was.”

The history separating the two societies is particularly painful. During World War II, tens of thousands of Polish civilians were killed by Ukrainian nationalist formations in the Volhynia region. Polish nationalist groups retaliated, killing thousands of Ukrainian civilians. The competing memories of these events have remained politically sensitive, especially in families whose relatives were victims.

After the fall of communism, the history of Volhynia became increasingly prominent in Polish public debate. In Ukraine, meanwhile, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) acquired an important place in national memory because of its role in the struggle for Ukrainian independence against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. Disputes over monuments, commemorations, exhumations and historical figures have repeatedly affected relations between Warsaw and Kyiv.

The subject is also vulnerable to manipulation, according to Łukasz Wojtkowski, an assistant professor at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, who researches information operations and disinformation. He argues that historical grievances can be connected to contemporary fears and used to deepen divisions: “Volhynia is a playbook for propaganda and disguised disinformation,” he explains. “It is basically the only open case between those two nations that can spark the engine of disinformation and hatred. Russia can put two irons in the fire at the same time: it can increase the hatred between Poland and Ukraine, and it can reinforce the Russian narrative that there is a fascist regime in Kyiv.”

Anna Mierzyńska, a Polish journalist and social media researcher specialising in disinformation, has studied similar narratives targeting Polish audiences. “Reliable historical debate,” she stresses, “is always based on listening to both sides and taking new developments into account. Its purpose is not to attack or create hatred, but to explain what happened and find an understanding.” While there is such a debate among historians and experts, she adds that in the Polish information sphere, “many of the posts on this subject are designed to provoke hatred toward Ukrainians.”

Recurring narratives portray Ukrainians as a physical threat to Poles, Mierzyńska continues, using descriptions of the Volhynia crimes to create fear, or to suggest that Ukrainians could seek Polish territory. Existing social problems can also be folded into the same narrative. Long waiting lists for healthcare, for example, existed before the arrival of millions of Ukrainian refugees, but online claims blamed Ukrainians for them. Housing, employment and public services have been framed in similar ways.

The scale of Ukrainian displacement makes the relationship especially important. In 2026, nearly a million Ukrainians took temporary protection in Poland, representing 21.8 percent of all people from Ukraine under temporary protection in the European Union.

We need good contacts between Poles and Ukrainians, integration, getting to know each other and building trust. When we know each other well and trust each other, outside influence becomes much less important. – Anna Mierzyńska

For Piotrowski, the first months after the invasion demonstrated what such contact can look like. “Ordinary citizens living on the border with Ukraine were the first ones to provide immediate support,” he recalls. “I have never seen so much kindness in my life on both sides of the border, and so much reconciliation and understanding.”

Five years into the full-scale war, however, the border has also revealed the limits of that extraordinary solidarity. “I understand that when Poles opened their homes, it could become difficult,” Piotrowski says. “Someone comes who speaks another language, has slightly different customs and wants to stay for a long time. This is what I call empathy burnout.”

He does not regard that exhaustion as proof that the solidarity of 2022 was false, but rather, as a relationship being tested by time. His response is the same one that drives Folkowisko’s cultural work: more contact. “Poles don't know Ukrainians, Ukrainians don't know Poles,” he says. “Our job is to make people meet each other and understand each other.”

This approach means bringing difficult history into conversations in much the same way that Folkowisko’s festivals and programmes bring Polish and Ukrainian participants together while addressing the violence and displacement that transformed the region.

Wojtkowski is more cautious about whether historical reconciliation alone could resolve the wider conflict over competing narratives. “Imagine that tomorrow Poland and Ukraine commemorate every victim, Ukraine admits who was killed and how many people died, Poland admits what happened on its side, and all the exhumations are completed,” he posits. “It would not change everything, because Russia has other narratives.”

He maintains that, when it comes to history, both Polish and Ukrainian society did not do their homework properly. “In Poland, we learned the story of the interwar period as the restoration of the Polish state after more than a hundred years without independence,” he says, “but we did not always learn enough about the Ukrainian experience within that state. Ukraine has its own work to do in confronting everything that happened during the Second World War.”

Wojtkowski further advises that both Poland and Ukraine “should step very carefully, as if on very thin ice.” According to him, there should be signs of goodwill and a willingness to cooperate, but there is still a lot to do politically, academically and socially.

For Piotrowski, however, governments and historians do not have to resolve everything before ordinary people can build relationships: “We are trying to connect people who live ten or 15 kilometres from each other. They have different memories, different histories, but they can still meet and work together.”

As Ukraine moves toward the European Union, and as Polish and Ukrainian lives become increasingly intertwined, those everyday relationships may shape how the two societies handle their shared past. “If we lose the contact between ordinary people across both countries,” Piotrowski maintains, “then it becomes much easier to build the walls. And once the walls are there, it is much harder to build the bridges again.”

articles.title: Vote young yet govern much later: West African youth’s struggle for power
articles.author: Laura
paras: In all of West Africa, te voting age is 18, but presidential eligibility ages vary widely
Originally published on Global Voices
Youth mobilized in Africa. Screenshot from DW Africa's YouTube channel

In West Africa, young people can vote for the first time at 18. In some states, they are eligible to serve in parliament by age 25. However, depending on the country, they must wait until they are 35, 40, or even 50 years old before being eligible to run for the highest office. Although these age limits are beginning to shift, the real challenges often lie deeper in the electoral structure.

Young people are deemed mature enough to elect their leaders, yet not to replace them. They drive political movements forward by voting, advocating, campaigning, and protesting, yet cannot run for office themselves. The question is, can democracy really be called inclusive when it gives young people the right to elect but not to be elected?

Across the region, the voting age is 18. However, presidential eligibility ages vary widely. In Gambia, it’s 30; in Senegal, Nigeria, and Côte d’Ivoire, it’s 35; and in Benin, Ghana, and Guinea, it’s 40. In the legislative assemblies, the bar is even lower. In Togo, Benin, Senegal, and Nigeria’s House of Representatives, it’s 25, while in Ghana it’s 21.

The situation in Togo requires closer inspection. On May 6, 2024, the country legally became a parliamentary republic. Under the 2024 Constitution, the eligibility age for President of the Republic is 50. Parliament also now elects the president, whose powers are limited. Authority now rests with the President of the Council of Ministers, who must be at least 40 and is not elected in public presidential elections. Faure Gnassingbé has held this position since May 3, 2025, the day parliament also elected the country’s oldest-ever incoming president of the Republic, Jean-Lucien Savi de Tové, 86.
However, the country’s legal age limit is hardly set in stone. In 2002, the National Assembly lowered it from 45 to 35 — a reform the opposition called tailor-made for Faure Gnassingbé.

More recently, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, on July 30, 2026, the Ghanaian government agreed in principle to lower the minimum presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35, defying the Constitutional Review Committee’s recommendation of 30. This legislation will ultimately go to a referendum, requiring a 40 percent turnout and a 75 percent approval.

In 2018, Nigeria set a regional precedent. Under pressure from the youth-led Not Too Young To Run campaign, the law lowered the presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35 and the House of Representatives’ eligibility age from 30 to 25.

According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union, lowering the minimum presidential age leads to younger parliaments. However, Côte d’Ivoire tells a very different story. In 2016, after removing the maximum age limit of 75 to run for office, incumbent President Alassane Ouattara, 83, ran for another term in 2025. The law rarely protects younger generations.
Youths particularly active in street movements

Even though young people have the right to vote across the continent, that does not mean all young people exercise that right. In August 2025, an Afrobarometer survey found that those aged 18 to 35 were less active than their elders in almost all traditional means of political participation. Overall across the continent, they trailed by 18 percentage points in voting, but by a record 29 points in Senegal. Protests were the only exception.

In Togo’s capital of Lomé, the June 6 Movement, sparked by the rapper Aamron’s arrest, brought thousands of people onto the streets. According to the Media Foundation for West Africa, the subsequent crackdown, for which the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) blamed government-backed militiamen, left seven dead.

Similarly, in Madagascar, the September 2025 protests toppled President Andry Rajoelina’s government, resulting in a military takeover. According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), the overthrown president himself came to power in 2019 on the back of a protest, at just 34 years old.

Comparably, in Kenya, street protests forced the withdrawal of the 2024 Finance Bill. Meanwhile, in Morocco, youth-led protests prompted the authorities to announce youth candidacy incentives and prosecute specific ringleaders.
Although leaderless movements wrest concessions, they rarely last without political parties or trade unions to sustain them.
The gap between participation and representation

The Inter-Parliamentary Report, published on April 9, 2026, found that elected officials aged 30 and under account for just 2.8 percent of all parliamentarians worldwide. Since 2023, progress has stalled for the first time since 2014. More than a third (37.1 percent) of legislative houses have no parliamentarians in this age group.

The lack of youth representation and participation is a significant challenge considering young people under 35 account for roughly 70 percent of West Africa’s population, according to the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference.

According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), at the start of Ghana’s 2025 parliamentary term, despite the legal minimum age of 21, no parliamentarians were aged 30 or under. What’s more, those aged 31 to 40 held just 46 of the 269 parliamentary seats, or 17.1 percent. After Senegal’s 2024 legislative elections, the National Assembly had only five members under 30, accounting for just 3 percent. Although almost 38 percent of registered voters were aged 18 to 35, the Assembly’s average age was 47. Elected at just 44, the country’s youngest-ever president, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, only became an official candidate after his mentor, Ousmane Sonko, was disqualified.

In Nigeria, International IDEA, an intergovernmental organization that supports sustainable democracy worldwide, reported that in 2015, only three of the 360 members of the House of Representatives were between the ages of 18–25, rising to 14 in 2019 — a positive but modest development.
In Dakar, the head of Yiaga Africa, the organization behind the Not Too Young to Run campaign, summed up the situation, stating that the political arena is more open on paper than in reality.

However, Afrobarometer has identified a paradox. While young people do vote less than their elders, they are also excluded from seats of power and the polls. This representation gap is anything but passive; it breeds disengagement. The IPU warns that young people’s absence from parliamentary assemblies undermines institutional legitimacy and jeopardizes trust in democracy. Senegal, listed in the 2026 IPU report as one of the countries where parliament grew younger in the most recent elections, shows that rejuvenation is possible when a political agenda empowers a generation.
Rewriting the deal: money, parties, obstacles

High age limit proponents demand experience. Across the 34 countries that Afrobarometer surveyed, citizens favor an average leadership age of 39. Those calling for a lower age limit seek proven engagement measures, such as lowering the eligibility age, quotas, and forums for young parliamentarians. However, as Nigeria shows, often, the main obstacle is financial.

Nigeria’s ruling party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), has set the total cost of its 2027 presidential nomination and expression-of-interest forms at NGN 100 million (USD 75,000), NGN 30 million (USD 22,521) for the expression of interest, and NGN 70 million (USD 52,550) for the nomination. The Senate will cost NGN 20 million (USD 15,014) and the House of Representatives NGN 10 million (USD 7,507).

Young people will receive a 50 percent discount only on nomination fees, leaving the presidential bill at NGN 65 million (USD 48,789). A Nigerian civil society group calculated that workers earning the minimum wage, NGN 70,000 (USD 52) per month, would have to work for more than a century to buy some of these forms.

The Electoral Act, 2026, signed on February 18, also doubled the presidential candidate’s campaign spending limit to NGN 10 billion (USD 7.5 million) and tripled that of governorship candidates to NGN 3 billion (USD 2.2 million).

At the initiative of ECOWAS and the youth-led advocacy organization Legis360, delegates from 12 countries gathered in Dakar to bring these obstacles to the forefront. In their communiqué, they launched the West Africa Youth Observer Network (WAYON) and called for youth quotas, reduced candidate fees, and spending limits. ECOWAS later announced it would deploy youth-only election observers for Nigeria’s upcoming presidential election on January 16, 2027.

Other countries exemplify how laws can directly impact nominations. According to the IPU, Ecuador owes much of its progress to a 2022 law, which required 25 percent of its candidates to be young adults. Countries with term limits also have considerably more young parliamentarians than the global average. In 2023, the IPU also noted that limited youth funding and a lack of spending limits contributed to aging parliamentary assemblies.

Elsewhere, the obstacles are political. Take, for example, Benin. After disqualifying the main opposition candidate (Les Démocrates) for failing to meet election requirements, current President Romuald Wadagni faced only one opponent (Paul Hounkpe). On April 12, 2026, Wadagni subsequently won the presidential election with 94.27 percent of the vote. In 2024, a constitutional reform that extended the presidential term from five to seven years also raised the minimum vote threshold for securing seats in the National Assembly from 10 percent of parliamentary election votes to 20 percent. This regulation far outweighs a candidate’s date of birth when they have no party machine behind them.

Another example is Burkina Faso. In January 2026, the military junta dissolved all political parties. Meanwhile, in The Gambia, President Barrow will run for a third term in the December 5 presidential election.
Inclusive voting, but flawed representation

Is a system that gives young people the right to elect their leader but impedes their ability to become one themselves fully inclusive? The findings speak for themselves. Although Nigeria has lowered its age limits and Ghana has committed to doing the same, these limits are more a symptom than a cause. Age is not the sole contributing factor.

Critics argue that lowering age limits without also addressing nomination costs, party regulations, and the openness of the political arena would only be the first step on a seemingly endless staircase. What stands between young people and decision-making positions are exceedingly high costs, restrictive nomination practices, candidate exclusions, and even the lack of parties.

Until street movements have credible institutional representatives, they will continue to wrest temporary concessions or, as seen in Madagascar, give way to powers other than those they had hoped for. The primary challenge of the West African Democratic Pact is making young people not only the promised future of politics, but also an active part of today’s representation.

articles.title: In opting for Lula, Brazil made a conservative choice to elect a man of the left over one of the far right
articles.author: João Gabriel de Lima, Jornalista, doutorando em Política Comparada, Universidade de Lisboa
paras: The 2026 elections in Brazil played out amid an widespread assumption repeated around the world: that the country was polarized and that would inform the vote.

But the word “polarization” implies symmetry – and symmetry is something that never existed in the contest between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. On one side, a moderate center-left politician with a center-right running mate, Geraldo Alckmin. On the other, a representative of the radical right and a member of an international movement that critics say threatens democracies around the world.

Flávio is no mere conservative. While he may be courted and supported by the members of the Republican Party in the U.S., his policies put him more in the mold of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany and Portugal’s Enough, a party that advocates the repatriation of immigrants and a ban on Muslim places of worship.

On the day he launched his candidacy, at an event of Brazil’s Liberal Party (PL) in São Paulo, Flávio laid out three of the guiding principles of what his administration would look like. First was the so called “Project Darkness”, a crime-fighting plan inspired by by El Salvador’s hard-right President Nayib Bukele. Second was joining the Shield of the Americas, U.S. President Donald Trump’s military and political initiative for the continent. Thirdly, Flávio laid out plans for the “tesouraço” or “big cut” – a slashing of public spending modeled after Argentinian President Javier Milei’s “chainsaw” economic policy. Since he didn’t provide any details, it’s unclear whether it would be just as sharp as Milei’s, but it was enough to strike fear into those who depend on social programs to survive.

Milei himself was at the launch event. He arrived singing the song The Panic Show by the Argentine hard rock band La Renga. Flávio accompanied Milei in the song’s refrain: “Yo soy el león, soy el rey y te destrozaré” (“I am the lion, I am the king, and I will tear you apart”) while dancing along with the Argentine president.

It is, I believe, the form, more than the content, that defines the members of the far-right brotherhood that threatens democracies around the world. They are politicians who do not like to negotiate, even though negotiation is the essence of politics. They want to annihilate the “enemy”, as if they were, literally, on a battlefield.

Flávio’s ideas are clearly “misplaced ideas,” to borrow the term coined by Brazilian literary critic, essayist, and professor Roberto Schwarz. It is impossible to implement Nayib Bukele’s crime-fighting plan — which allows for the arrest of any citizen without a formal charge, the right for legal counsel, or habeas corpus — in a democratic country.

On the economy side, in the midst of a debt crisis, Brazil does needs a fiscal adjustment. However, the country’s economic situation bears no resemblance to that of Argentina, a country that has seen its currency collapse and is rolling over dollar denominated debt.

A recent report in the Financial Times portrayed what is known in Brazil as Bolsonarism as a clan similar to the Roy family from the American television series “Succession.” Nothing could be more apt. Flávio is not Flávio. He is merely a generic offshoot of the Bolsonaro brand. During the Brazilian TV Globo election debate held right before the runoff of last Sunday, Oct. 25, he referred to his now jailed father administration as “our government.” If he were elected president, Flávio would have governed under Jair’s supervision and alongside his brother Eduardo Bolsonaro - a former congressman now living in the U.S. to escape a arrest warrant - who serves as the point of contact between Bolsonarism and the radical and far right around the world.

Eduardo is close to former Hungary prime minister Viktor Orbán, Spain’s Santiago Abascal, president of Spanish far-right party Vox, El Salvador’s Bukele, France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen, and the most radical wing of the U.S. Republican Party.

Flávio spent the election campaign trying to pretend he wasn’t like his father. He marketed himself as the “moderate Bolsonaro.” But Bolsonarism, in Brazilian politics, is synonymous with extremism. The mask slipped during his final speech. If he were a democrat, he would have conceded the indisputable defeat suffered on Oct. 25. Instead, he refused to concede and vowed to challenge the results.

But how did Lula defeat Flávio? My hypothesis is that Brazilians made a conservative choice. Lula has already governed the country three times. Voters know what to expect from him. His opponent, on the other hand, is seen widely as the Brazilian member of a radical global right wing movement, and whose leader is in prison for attempting a coup. The images of vandals destroying the buildings that house the federal executive, legislative, and judicial branches of Brazil’s government on 8 Jan. 2023 – an echo of the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol riot in the U.S. – are still vivid in the memory of Brazilians.
Faced with a choice between something they already know and the unpredictability of extremists, Brazilians opted for the conservative vote. Being prudent, they did not want to risk their democracy.

articles.title: The upside of untidiness: why a little mess can be good for your home
articles.author: Jamal Abarashi, Lecturer, Marketing and International Business Department, Auckland University of Technology
paras: If we’re to follow the philosophy of organiser extraordinaire Marie Kondo, a tidy home is a better home.

Albert Einstein, however, might have contested that point. “If a cluttered desk is a sign of a cluttered mind,” goes a quote widely attributed to the famed physicist, “of what, then, is an empty desk a sign?”
My newly published research, which studied 22 New Zealand households, also challenges the conventional wisdom that mess is a problem which must be fixed.
Far from being a symptom of poor organisation, mess can help families function and make life run more smoothly.
When mess makes life easier
Consider the spaces in our homes that serve more than one purpose, and where things tend to pile up. A living room that doubles as a play area, or a bedroom that also serves as a study.

One couple told me how their dining table becomes a “drop zone” for belongings such as bags and drink bottles, before it’s cleared each evening. Another person described how leaving something on his kitchen island made him less likely to forget it when leaving the house.

Disorderly as each of those spaces might have appeared, they served daily routines which might have been disrupted for the sake of a tidier-looking home. We might think of clutter as stuff that simply gets in our way. But often, a messy space is just one that is being useful to us.

For one mum, her kitchen counter served as a dining table and a workspace for her and her daughter. Pens, toys and other items might accumulate, but “as long as there’s still space to eat, then I kind of just let it be”.

Mess can also tell us much about family relationships. One dad would leave his daughter’s jumper hanging on the back of a chair rather than pack it away. She had previously left it on the floor, and he wanted to acknowledge her progress. “So I regard that as a win,” he said.

Another person told me she put up with some of her partner’s mess because “he also lives here”. For her, a shared home should not be organised only around one person’s idea of tidiness. Leaving some things alone was a way of recognising that the space belonged to both of them.
These might be modest examples, but they show us that the seemingly simple act of tidying can run up against the encouragement we offer our children or the respect we show our partners.
When we’re making room for other people’s ways of living, putting everything in its “proper” place sometimes isn’t the most considerate thing to do.
So, should we just stop tidying and embrace chaos? Not quite.

Previous research has linked household clutter to stress, embarrassment and conflict between family members. Mess can make things harder to find, prevent us from using a space or create more work for someone else.
Our study doesn’t dispute these problems. Rather, it suggests we need to look beyond how messy a space appears to understand whether that mess is actually causing difficulties.
We found households used three main approaches to managing disorder: clearing things away, tolerating them or simply hiding them from view.

One woman described pushing her partner’s golf balls and other belongings beneath a cabinet, where they were less visible. Another kept her daily supplements on the kitchen counter rather than in the pantry, because putting them away might mean she forgot to take them.

These decisions reflect something earlier research has tended to overlook: keeping a home tidy involves balancing different needs, routines and expectations. What one person regards as clutter might be important to someone else’s daily life.

Our findings also suggest tidiness is rarely a permanent state. Spaces become messy as people use them, are cleared when needed, then become messy again. Trying to maintain constant order can mean repeatedly undoing arrangements that serve a useful purpose.

This doesn’t mean all mess should be tolerated. But a home that looks perfectly organised isn’t necessarily one that works best for the people living in it. Perhaps the better measure of a well-organised home isn’t how tidy it looks, but how well it works for the people who live there.

articles.title: Israeli election: why nobody has been talking about Palestinian statehood
articles.author: Amnon Aran, Professor of International Relations, City St George's, University of London
paras: As Israelis head to the polls on October 27 one major issue that has not received serious attention during the campaign is Israel’s flat rejection of Palestinian statehood.

This puts Israel seriously at odds with world opinion. As it stands, 159 countries around the world recognise Palestinian statehood, including diplomatic heavyweights such as the UK and France. The two UN security council members joined Australia, Andorra, Canada, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, Portugal and San Marino in formally recognising the state of Palestine in September 2025.

This represents an important shift within the world’s most important diplomatic frameworks. Now, nearly half of the G7 and four of the five permanent members of the UN security council – China, France, Russia and the UK – recognise Palestine as a legitimate state.

This international pressure was recently ramped up by international sanctions by the UK and others against Israeli settler groups. Given this pressure – as well as the ongoing conflict in Gaza – you’d expect opposition parties, at least, to engage with the record of the Netanyahu government on the Palestinian question. But there is silence. Not only from the government, but also from the opposition parties hoping to replace it.

The political parties comprising the ultra-nationalist government of the incumbent Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, champion “destroying Hamas”. They continue to flatly reject the notion of Palestinian statehood – to the contrary, they enthusiastically promote the expansion of Israeli settlements.

Netanyahu’s extreme-right partners, who he has depended on to keep him in power, include the Religious Zionism party of finance minister Belazel Smotrich, and national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power. These two parties want to go further. Their election campaign advocates the occupation of the whole of the West Bank. They back this with a euphemistically branded plan for “voluntary Palestinian emigration”.

The key contenders to replace Netanyahu are Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of Yashar (Straight), and Naftali Bennet, the leader of B'Yachad (Together). They have diverged from the Netanyahu government’s policy by promising to bring order to the West Bank by curbing settler violence. They both reject the idea of expanding settlements and promoting Palestinian emigration.

Eisenkot, widely seen as the most likely candidate to beat Netanyahu, says he is in favour of settlements that comply with Israeli law. He has also been a harsh critic of the massive E1 settlement. This is the massive proposed project which would – if completed – effectively cut the West Bank in half and make a Palestinian state all but impossible. Both Eisenkot and Bennet share the Netanyahu government’s stance of flatly rejecting Palestinian statehood.
The fact that Israeli political leadership is so out of step with world opinion on Palestinian statehood raises some pressing questions.

It was in September that the UK and 11 other countries announced a package of sanctions in response to settler violence and the signing off by Netanyahu’s government of the E1 plan. The sanctions directly target produce, goods and services from or associated with illegal settlements.

There has been discussion within the European Union of a broader package of sanctions, which could include stripping Israel of its preferred trading-nation status. In response, Netanyahu suggested that Israel might respond by using cryptocurrencies and blockchain technologies to evade such restrictions. This drew a stern rebuke from Israel’s central bank, which said: “The right course of action for the Israeli economy is to preserve economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy”.

Another big concern arising from the growing turmoil on the West Bank and the ongoing conflict in Gaza is the pressure this is putting on the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF). The IDF chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, recently issued a stark warning that the military already faces a manpower crisis. “I am raising ten red flags before the IDF collapses into itself,” Zamir reportedly told a security cabinet meeting. As well as its deployment in Gaza and across the West Bank and on Israel’s borders, the IDF also has troops in southern and southwestern Syria and southern Lebanon.
Despite the high stakes, the main parties contesting the Israeli elections appear to have no answers to these pressing questions.
Palestinian statehood is not an election winner

Opinion polls suggest the apparent lack of interest in a long-term solution for Palestinian self-determination may be a calculated strategy. There has been a significant shift in voter sentiment in Israel since Hamas’ October 7 deadly attacks. Many voters – particularly younger Israelis – are taking a hardline view towards Palestinians and Palestinian statehood. More than 16% of first-time voters are planning to support the far-right parties of Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, according to a poll for one of Israel’s most popular newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth.

The majority of people in Israel reject the idea of a two-state solution. Many also see the growing international criticism of Israel as hypocrisy and evidence of a rise in antisemitism around the world. The key issues at the ballot box remain security, cost of living and who is to blame for the October 7 attacks.

The latest polling, which combines surveys by three of Israel’s major TV networks, has a possible Eisenkot coalition marginally ahead with 54 seats to 50 for a likely Netanyhu-led coalition. The margin is about 16 seats, reflecting the number of people who declare themselves undecided.

Once the votes are counted and a ruling coalition is formed, it’ll be for the next Israeli leader and whoever they choose to form a coalition with to work out how to deal with the serious challenges posed by the country’s growing isolation. It’s clear enough that the Palestinian question is at the heart of that. But the election campaign has offered no clues about how a future government might deal with it.

articles.title: ‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power
articles.author: Gavin Brent Sullivan, Professor of Social Psychology, International Psychoanalytic University Berlin
paras: Serbia’s student-led political movement has secured a historic election victory. Preliminary results suggest the so-called Student List has won 141 of the 250 seats in parliament, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party taking 104. The result brings the 12-year rule of Alexander Vučić to an end.

The Student List’s story is remarkable. It has no standalone leader and fielded candidates without political experience from across Serbian society. Stemming from student-led protests against the entrenched corruption and creeping authoritarianism of the ruling regime, it has now achieved an improbable dream.

In late 2025, one of us (Gavin Brent Sullivan) conducted focus groups with members of the student protest movement as part of the Pledge EU Horizon project. The project explores the emotional dynamics of political grievances and their democratic implications.

The protesters’ grievances were centred on the 2024 collapse of a roof at the newly renovated Novi Sad train station in northern Serbia, which killed 16 people. Allegations of state involvement through corruption in the procurement process and lowered building standards have been denied by the government. But they nonetheless sparked large nationwide protests.

Focus group participants expressed anger and underlying fear about harassment during the protests by what they said were government-funded gangs. They also spoke of their concern at the threats and violence directed towards them, not only as they protested but also when walking in areas near government buildings in main cities. Several students reported feeling threatened even in their own homes.

At the same time, the students voiced dissatisfaction with teachers who were not supportive of their movement, and other students who opposed them. This dissatisfaction extended to older family members and relatives who repeated government-controlled media fabrications about the protests. These included claims that the students were being paid by foreign anti-Serbian groups.

Despite the fear of arrest or worse, and despondency that change could really occur, the students who took part in the focus groups were resilient. They were focused on their long-term goal of regime change, with many students talking with pride about creating a leaderless movement that was organising candidates to challenge Vučić in an election.

Several participants reported feeling spontaneous, intense experiences of national pride when taking part in the protests. Some spoke of taking back national symbols such as the Serbian flag to counter propaganda that they were not patriotic and wanted to destroy the country.
Feelings of solidarity were also experienced when minority Bosniak Muslim students from Novi Pazar University in south-western Serbia joined the protests. As one participant said:

They’re a minority which was at odds with Serbia, with Serbian nationals actually. So now we had that part of reunification with them and they’re a Muslim minority. They are really active in these protests and student protests and it’s been wonderful.

Another member of the focus group noted that they expected elections to be “brutal”. But they were optimistic about the prospect of unseating the Vučić government. They said: “I see the glimpse of hope that this is our future and that actually we can say to our kids, our grandkids, we changed the system, we were the change.”

At the same time, most of the students did not dare to dream that they would succeed in ousting a government that had held a 12-year grip on power. It is stunning now after Vučić’s concession speech in which he admitted “it is clear that we have lost these elections” to know that they were successful just one year later.

The remarkable victory of the Student List should give hope to any group opposing a corrupt, authoritarian regime that a core commitment to democracy is precisely what attracts voters to choose progressive change.

However, while there will be euphoria, pride and tears of joy in Serbia as the election result sinks in, there may also be groups who are fearful of change and that the new government may seek accountability for members of the ousted regime. Some theorists of political emotions talk about the possibility for revenge to be enacted by winners, especially when a fight for power has been bitter.

For those on the losing side, meanwhile, electoral defeat can bring grief, anxiety and anger. But acknowledging these emotions and coming to terms with loss can bring openness to change. In his concession speech, Vučić said: “I do not want unrest, I do not want killings, I do not want anything like that on the streets.”

The Student List’s commitment to democracy, pluralism and justice should also override any desire for redress. The movement has actively avoided developing a victim identity, taking responsibility for enacting change themselves.
As one focus group participant said:

Of course, they [the government] are the problem. I’m not trying to deny that. But I would blame us more … because, I mean, we chose them, we keep choosing them. Okay, they do steal when it comes to the elections, they do many things, they hide, they try to control the media and everything. But at the same time, we don’t have the opposition and we have that state of mind that is allowing them to do everything they’re doing.

There are various other challenges facing the Student List. These include adapting the movement’s leaderless organisational assemblage into a government capable of delivering the reforms required for EU membership.

But regardless of what happens next, it was certainly a privilege to talk to the students at a time when change did not seem possible and to provide encouragement and support when there was little outside recognition of their struggles and sacrifices.
